en: Chapter One: Introduction;
Visualization of Five-Faced, Sixteen-Armed Bhairava
Oṃ, homage to Mahābhairava!
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
crowded with perfected yogis, endowed with various trees,
filled with throngs of Apsarases, and served by Yakṣas and Gandharvas.
In that place crowded with various [beings], variegated with diverse minerals,
filled with many peaks, and frequented by hosts of *gaṇas* and *gandharvas*,
he possessed the luster of molten gold, endowed with the brilliance of the thousand-rayed sun.
Resorted to by the ṛṣis and frequented by hosts of siddhas,
it was filled with groves of *karṇikāra* trees and blossoming *campaka* flowers;
it was further adorned with *sarja*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* trees, as well as *pāṭalī* and *aśoka* trees.
There, on that delightful mountain, he remained together with Umā;
[he was seated] upon a wonderful golden throne inlaid with jewels,
[serving] the five-faced God who wears a garland of skulls.
Object: Confusion (moha).
TiUdgh 1.7ab: Endowed with sixteen arms, and at that time, having two eyes;
TiUdgh 1.7cd: With matted hair bound into an upward-pointing crown, and having the moon as his crest-ornament.
With tawny hair, most terrible, blazing like a fire,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, and adorned with large nostrils and earrings.
With bracelets,
armlets, and waistbands, the Lord of the Gods shines, bearing half of Umā’s body;
the God who wields the sword as his limb and is formidable with the trident in hand.
[The one] who bears the great [trident], the Hero, likewise holding a vajra and a sword;
with a spear and an axe in his hands, adorned with a rosary of beads;
and whose lotus-like hand holds a great corpse, its ear well-adorned.
In the Mahāśvakara [mudrā], the food is filled to the brim with well-prepared [offerings].
With an elephant hide as an upper garment, and terrifying with a bell in his hand.
Because he is clothed in a tiger skin, he is difficult to behold even for the gods.
With eyes like hollows and great weapons, adorned with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā),
licking his great tongue, he is the creator of the emission of saṃsāra.
In his left hand he holds a skull-cup, and likewise a *ḍamaru* drum in his [other] hand;
he has a discus in his hand, as well as a bow, and likewise an arrow raised in his hand. [He holds] a lotus...
And likewise, the Bhaṭṭārikā, resting upon his hand,
laughing with shouts of joy and letting out a great, terrifying laugh.
Assuming the form of Bhairava and surrounded by great yogis,
he thus [experiences] bliss...
[[one folio missing]]

Just as the nectar of a Kaulika is to a fool, or the true essence of the scriptures [is to one who lacks it], so too is the pleasure of a maiden’s woman to a most wicked man who turns his back upon the Kaulika.
But those who are deluded by ignorance and bewildered by the web of scriptures do not know the supreme bliss, the nectar of the knowledge of Kula.

O Goddess, that which bestows the accomplishment of one's desires is presided over by the power of will (icchā-śakti); by whatever form it may be established, or by whatever vow, or wherever there may be conduct— whether dualistic, non-dualistic, or according to one's wish.

But when the opportunity arises, whether I am a householder or a celibate student, whether clothed or formless, or however I may be situated according to my wish, or wherever I may be located— then I speak as if it were sacrificial porridge.
O Queen of the Gods, even so, one who is more venerable than the guru himself does not attain perfection through the immersion in the power of Rudra [if he is] not born of the Kaula womb; rather,
he attains perfection through Kaula yoga.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Darkness.
Bhairava said: [Chapter 3 praises the Kaula tradition over the vaineya (ordinary Śaiva)].
TimUdgh 3.1ab: In this world, one speaks of the meaning of the texts while acting otherwise oneself; TimUdgh 3.1cd: [Such] knowledge, made arrogant by scholars, has led to an evil destiny.
TimUdgh 3.2ab: Satisfied with the mere literal meaning, they contemplate the meaning of the Vedic scriptures.
The one deluded by the pursuit of wealth does not find the supreme peace;
how can there be knowledge for such a person, even through hundreds of millions of texts?
Like camphor, saffron, and other such things carried by a donkey, it is useless.

TimUdgh 3.4ab: And many, deluded, having been cast out by those who are unestablished in discipline (*vinaya*), TimUdgh 3.4cd: do not find the bliss of the Kaula lineage (*kaulakrānanda*), O fair-faced one.

TimUdgh 3.5ab: Men who are satisfied with the *mantras* and *tantras*, having gained some slight experiential realization; TimUdgh 3.5cd: And who, without attaining the *kaulika* knowledge, remain content with mere discipline (*vinaya*);
TimUdgh 3.6ab: [Those] established in white, yellow, and so forth...
Or else [one may use] something pungent and so forth. (TimUdgh 3.6cd) Kuṇḍalā is circular in shape; likewise, there is Dahanāpyāyanā.
(TimUdgh 3.7ab) And similarly, there are others such as these, as well as another called Bhūtaśuddhi. (TimUdgh 3.7cd)
TimUdgh 3.7cd: Bindu, nāda, as well as śakti, and the subtle path itself; [these are the stages of *uccāra*.

TimUdgh 3.8ab: Having understood the rule of the principle of knowledge (*jñānatattva*), men who were dissatisfied with the Śaiva [tradition], TimUdgh 3.8cd: all became attached to the Kaulika [path] of the great-souled Yoginīs.

TimUdgh 3.9ab: Likewise, those who are to be converted (*vaineyika*) are proclaimed to be like insects and the state of cattle. TimUdgh 3.9cd: And they are like golden and earthen [images], as are the elephant and the mosquito.

TimUdgh 3.10ab: O Goddess, by such a measure is the Kaula-vaineyika [to be understood]. (Note: The syntax of this passage is defective; it presumably intends to compare the gold and the elephant [to the Kaula practitioner].)
And like clay and a mosquito to one who is to be converted (vaineya). As an elephant [is not seen] in the sky where the supreme moon is grasped,
so it is, O Lord of the Kaulas (Kaulīśa), that you shine while wandering upon the surface of the earth.
TimUdgh 3.11cd: Conjoined with the syllables of the Passionate One (*rañjita*) and endowed with the syllables of the Kaula Vidyā;
TimUdgh 3.12ab: The Yoga of the Cintāmaṇi of Meditation is inconceivable...
[folio missing].
Chapter 4: How Śakti Manifests (along with its symptoms) in the Body TiUdgh04.1ab:
O Mahādeva, how does [Śakti] come to be in the body? TiUdgh04.1cd: This is my great doubt; tell me this, O Lord of the Gods.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, she is all-pervading within the hearts of all embodied beings;
awakened by the jewel of the instruction of knowledge, she becomes enlightened.
TiUdgh 04.3ab: He who, in his all-pervading form, is beheld as the union of Śiva and Śakti;

TiUdgh 04.3cd: O Goddess, this is the power of Rudra, which resides in the mouth of the Guru of the descent [of grace]. TiUdgh 04.4ab: That which they call the inconceivable is Śiva, the supreme cause.
From that [state], the power (śakti) emerges as Īśāna, which pierces through the *nāda* and the *bindu*.
By the mere utterance of that, realization arises;
and from the mass of karma, its paralysis (*stobha*) is produced.
O Goddess, through these two practices, the divine state is found; O Goddess, the divine body is established therein.
O Goddess, within three months of that, there is the vision of the various Yoginīs. And the divine deities, O fair-faced one, are seen by him as he stands in his celestial chariot.

O Goddess, it proceeds according to practice and according to its creation; this is the seed of creation. (TiUdgh 04.7cd) First, the heart trembles, and there is the rising [of the breath] to the palate; the head also whirls—this is the characteristic sign of the transition of creation. (TiUdgh 04.8ab–cd)
One should rotate each one thus in the joints of the limbs and sub-limbs;
by the power of the Kaula-vidyā, this entire body is made to whirl. One should produce various transformations and states at will.
One should not fear those various [beings], for the Supreme Goddess sports there.
Neither by *bhūtas* nor by *piśācas*, nor is one afflicted by delusion;
even when obstructed by the day (*ahni*), one is released from suffering.
In the form of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), she becomes the Guru for the yogi;
in the body, she is the supreme (*parā*) one who brings about the bliss of passion and removes all sins.
She is [the source of] son, friend, wife, [happiness], wealth, and sleep.
Those whose minds have been tasted by yoga perceive that which is desired as undesirable;
O fair-faced one, even the divine gods seated in their celestial chariots behold this. Through the possession [brought about] by mantra and tantra, they perceive the insentient as desired.
The penetration by the power of Rudra, the eternal penetration, and the insentient state; union with the divine deities, which is the cause of supreme bliss;
and that which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation from the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The penetration of Rudra’s power arises within one’s perceptions of sound; O fair-faced one, he whose yoga is joined does not distinguish between day and night,
nor does he experience hunger or thirst, nor indeed any bodily affliction.
He experiences joy, contentment, and constant bliss;
endowed with consciousness, he performs various types of *mudrā*-bindings,
as well as trembling, singing, dancing, and many kinds of transformations.
Through the transformation of impurity, he effects that which is not self-made by the multitude;
and he shakes off that which resides in the body of the supreme power along with the mass of impurities,
[that which is] arisen from the unreal.
And it has been said: "By good fortune, [the world] does not proceed at all;
by the sign of yoga, one sees nothing, nor is one overcome by ignorance anywhere. If one were to be overcome, then one would certainly see [the truth]. (TiUdgh 4.21)
"Otherwise, one who knows thus does not proceed according to tens of millions of scriptures.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, "The Opening of the Cataract," in the *Kaulajñānopadeśa* and its rewards.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to that which pertains to the Kaula knowledge concerning the downward and upward [paths],
obtained through the instruction of the Guru, and which bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
TimUdgh 5.2ab: When knowledge has been transferred, then liberation is certain.
TimUdgh 5.2cd: Like a potter’s wheel, O Goddess, the cage of the body revolves. TimUdgh 5.3ab: For sentient beings who have entered the path, it is illuminated by the vigor of gnosis.
They enjoy various pleasures, [which] bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
[it effects] attraction, subjugation, inciting enmity, eradication, and even killing,
as well as honor from kings, and likewise paralysis, immobilization, and so forth.
For she produces conviction in this regard and bestows manifold accomplishment of speech;
moreover, she grants those very vidyās that are proclaimed in the mantra-tantras.

TimUdgh 5.6ab: Perfectly accomplished in all ritual actions (*karma*), she bestows the fruits of all rites; TimUdgh 5.6cd: She is the supreme among all tantras, differentiated according to all castes (*varṇa*).
TimUdgh 5.7ab: She is the auspicious *Mṛtasaṃjīvanī* (Reviver of the Dead), and she is beautiful in the rites of *stobha* and summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*).

TimUdgh 5.7cd: When she is yellow, she is known for immobilization; when accompanied by smoke, for eradication. TimUdgh 5.8ab: Black, she brings about the death of enemies; in battle, she is red in color. TimUdgh 5.8cd:
Resplendent with glory, she has the luster of a lotus, having abandoned [all else] through her beauty and splendor.
TimUdgh 5.9ab: Atomicity (aṇimā), lightness (laghimā), as well as greatness (mahimā) and attainment (prāpti);
TimUdgh 5.9cd: Sovereignty (prākāmya), the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), mastery (vaśitva), and the state of being wherever one desires (yatra-kāmāvasāyitā).
TimUdgh 5.10ab: Hearing, seeing, and touching—the eighth is proclaimed [as the power of] touch.
Through the power of the Kaula Vidyā, one shall come to possess the eightfold sovereign qualities (aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya). I shall now tell you, my dear, that from which these qualities arise.
And twelve verses have been taught, sealed as the vision of all [the sciences]. They have been spoken; they have been proclaimed. [Taught in all sciences?]
Or is it "said to be the essence (*sarvasvam*) of all schools"?
[The scribe should preserve this with effort; he should not write it down.]
O fair-faced one, if one does not recite these twelve verses within seven days, it shall pass from ear to ear; but having obtained them,
one attains perfection in this world, and the emission is the equal flavor of creation.
At that very moment, the Khecarī mudrā is bound; of this there is no doubt.
The single seed-syllable consists of emanation, and the single mudrā is indeed Khecarī.

He by whom these two are known is also established in the state of peace. Established in that state, the yogi may even perceive the three worlds. [All things] arise in an instant; knowledge of the three times would thus be possible.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Timirodghāṭana*.
[Now follows] the signs of the immersion into the power of Rudra (*rudraśaktisamāveśa*).
The Goddess said:
TimUdgh 6.1ab: What is that power which transmigrates, and what signs does it manifest? TimUdgh 6.1cd: Abiding within the body, it produces states of paralysis and transformations.
TimUdgh 6.2ab: How is she to be known when she has transmigrated, and what is she like once she has entered [the new body]?
TimUdgh 6.2cd: And how is the upward departure [attained], and how does one travel upwards and downwards?
TimUdgh 6.3ab: How is it to be known, and at what time does it grant success (*siddhi*)?
TimUdgh 6.3cd: What are the signs of one who has attained success? O Supreme Lord, Bhairava, tell me this. Bhairava said:
TimUdgh 6.4ab: That which exists in the form of the all-pervading [principle] within the cosmic egg, including all moving and unmoving things;
TimUdgh 6.4cd: having pervaded [it] from below to above, it is remembered as that which is all-pervasive.
TimUdgh 6.5ab: It is situated within and without the body, and resides in all living beings.

TimUdgh 6.5cd: Through the instruction of a true teacher, there is a transition into another body. TimUdgh 6.6ab: Abiding and moving upward and downward are the characteristics of the transition of the body.
TimUdgh 6.6cd: O fair-faced one, the downward movement is the transition of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), while the upward movement is creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
TimUdgh 6.7ab: The yoga proceeds in three ways, established in stillness and movement.
TimUdgh 6.7cd: In this manner, it should be pierced in sequence; one should indicate it by means of the three as one.
TimUdgh 6.8ab: Pervading the body from below to above, one should cause the Supreme Power (parāśakti) to enter.
But he who possesses these marks is known as a guru who bestows liberation (*mokṣada*). (Note:
*mokṣada* is a recognized category of *ācārya*.)
Is this what is intended here?
*Timodgha* 6.9ab: Having performed all the ritual services, whether with one's own body or with wealth;
*Timodgha* 6.9cd: That state known as "intent upon that" (tatpara-saṃjñāna) is to be grasped from the mouths of the gurus.
By means of the jewel of the Kaula instruction, the yogi should behold her of divine vision with eyes closed; then, through direct perception once again,
he beholds the Yoginī as a mere shadow, again and again.
And just as one practices yoga,
so does it proceed;
[the practitioner] perceives it in a black form.
Raudrī, though fierce, appears in a gentle form, adorned with various ornaments.
She stands both visible and invisible, and is perceived in manifold forms.
Abiding eternally in the intermediate space, everyone beholds the Mother.
In the form of Raudra-Bhairava, surrounded by many yogis, he—
the bliss of the Self— beholds the city of the Lord of Yoga (Yogeśvara) once the Kaulika jewel of yoga has been attained, O fair-faced one.
On this earth, there is no such substance that, having been given,
could bring about liberation. [Yet] the teacher who bestows the Kaula instruction— the giver of liberation— is difficult to find.
To him who would cut through *saṃsāra*, that supreme [teaching] should be given:
the divine nectar of *Kaula* knowledge, which resides within many divisions.
That has been briefly told by me; it is seen in tens of millions of divisions.
Within twenty-seven years, the Siddhakhecarī is said [to be attained];
O Lord of Yogins constantly devoted [to practice], he indeed succeeds very quickly.
"Thus, O beloved, everything that was asked by you has been explained by me.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Timirodghāṭana*.
[This concerns] the yogic vision of the triple world in the sky.
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, you have explained to us the Kaulayoga in great detail.
Now, having seen the divine forms in their proper sequence, how may liberation be attained?"
Bhairava said:
The lord of yogis, constantly engaged in practice, beholds the entire triple world;
he perceives the cosmic egg as distinct, and by ascending above it, he shall go to Śiva.
"But above? "And above?
TimUdgh 7.3ab: In the first [state], one sees form; at the end of sleep, when the eyes are closed, TimUdgh 7.3cd: through the yoga of constant practice, there is the direct perception of the gods.
Even by means of speech he hears them, as well as touch and even that which is odorless; the lord of yogins, however, is preeminent in power, his mind established in truth.
TimUdgh 7.5ab: O you of divine form, manifest yourself in the sky before all the world! TimUdgh 7.5cd: Cause wonder to arise; O wise one, cause whatever you desire to be done.
TimUdgh 7.6ab: [This teaching] is joined with the meaning of the *grantha* and united with the *Vedānta*.
She composes charming poetry, beautiful and adorned with poetic ornaments;
she agitates the entire world, being herself colored by the enchanting conduct of a courtesan; she brings about possession in both women and men, and her song is truly captivating.
TimUdgh 7.8ab: Established in divine yoga, the yogin perceives through the measurement of the mind;
TimUdgh 7.8cd: [He sees] the netherworld, the world of the nāgas, and the divine realms of the three worlds;
TimUdgh 7.9ab: And the various human [realms], as well as grasses, shrubs, and creepers.
Bipeds, quadrupeds, and aquatic creatures of many kinds;
delightful regions, districts, villages, and cities.
Various syllables and the intermediate space (antarikṣa) should be shown;
within that intermediate space,
other lamps, oceans, Nandana groves, and mountains [are to be seen].
TimUdgh 7.11cd: He sees yakṣiṇīs of various forms, and especially Āṭaṅkā;
TimUdgh 7.12ab: He beholds the celestial palaces of the moon and sun, and the world of Indra;
TimUdgh 7.12cd: As well as the delightful city of the Guardians of the Quarters, and likewise the cities of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
He who sets in motion activity in the celestial, human, and subterranean realms—
[they] show the supreme power (parāśakti), the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving,
along with the city of Rudra, the auspicious city of the five faces.
TimUdgh 7.14cd: That supreme Sadāśiva is presided over by Parāśakti. TimUdgh 7.15ab: Above him is Śiva, the peaceful one, established in an uninterrupted state.
TimUdgh 7.15cd: The cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) should be pierced by Śakti; having done so, one should go to the state beyond the supreme.
He who [is established] in the end of *śam* and the end of *mā*, having attained liberation and release,
shall obtain final emancipation.
TimUdgh 7.16cd: This has been told to you, O Goddess, in due order, as the higher-and-lower [teaching].
7.17ab: O Goddess, one established in Kaula Yoga shall swiftly attain the state of peace.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Timitodghāṭana*.
The five jewels (*pañcaratna*) of the Kaula teachings appear to be a parallel to the categories (*padārtha*) of the Siddhānta.
The Goddess said:
"Devoid of the syllables of mantra and vidyā, and lacking meditative concentration (*dhyeya*) and mental retention (*dhāraṇā*),
how can one who teaches the five jewels attain true knowledge?"
Bhairava said:
"In the descent of the Kaula creation,
the characteristic meaning of the supreme text is obtained through the instruction of Rudra's power within the mouths of the gurus."
TimUdgh 8.3ab: All mantra-tantras and the discursive elaborations on the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of the deities—here *kalpa* refers to the texts—[may exist].
TimUdgh 8.3cd: Yet they do not succeed, even if they are vast, if they are devoid of the power of Rudra.
TimUdgh 8.4ab: The heart of all vidyās is remembered as the supreme potency of mantra.

One who is intent on the potency of mantra but does not know the immersion into the power of Rudra (*rudraśakti*) does not attain success. The knowledge of the Kaulika, which is beyond writing, resides within the mouths of the gurus.

TimUdgh 8.5cd: It should be transmitted from ear to ear; for one who stands at a distance shall not transmit it. TimUdgh 8.6ab: One should [know] the meditation on knowledge and meditative absorption, as well as the instruction on yogic sound (nāda).
TimUdgh 8.6cd: One should have the instructions on the five jewels written down according to the meaning of the text.
TimUdgh 8.7ab: When the first jewel is attained, through practice, there is the destruction of gray hair.
TimUdgh 8.7cd: Blazing upward within the body, he reaches the supreme state (*parāvasthā*).
TimUdgh 8.8ab: By the power of the second jewel, the Guru is satisfied by the disciple.
Honored by the circle of Yoginīs, they are established wherever they may be. In the third [state], however, when power (*śakti*) is transferred into one's own body,
that one of great strength, established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), agitates all those who stand before him.
In the fourth [stage], having attained the siddhi of the earth-walker (bhūcarī), one goes forth again;
in the fifth, having bound the khecarīmudrā, one ascends upwards.
Having gone before the city of Umāmaheśvarī, one goes forth once more.

Dhyāna and samādhi are defined as follows: Dhyāna occurs when one does not think of anything; through samādhi, one attains the state of *manonmanī*. Established therein, the great yogi perceives the entire world.
Yoga is defined as follows: Yoga is that which is certain through practice, whether in a forest or even on a mountain;
freed from all dualities, the yogi quickly attains perfection.
Beheld by the power of the perfected Vidyā, it produces manifold effects:
the dispeller of evil, delusion, madness, as well as emaciation (or nourishment),
the gross, the short, the long, and the child, the old, and the young.
TimUdgh 8.15ab: "Stay in the midst of the blazing fire," [referring to] one who has transcended transition;
[should he stay] in the midst of the blazing fire?
No, not in the blazing fire.
With [the mantra of] Jālāgni-sūrya-vāta, one may arrest even great rivers;
and bodily afflictions and obstacles are likewise [arrested] when [the mantra] is placed on the lip at the junction.
But one should not attempt to grasp it here; it revolves within one's own body.
Perfected in yoga, it sports with manifold conceptual forms.
TimUdgh 8.17cd: Whatever has been done by whatever means throughout all the worlds; TimUdgh 8.18ab: Whatever is yet to come in the future, or whatever fear is capable of arising from others.
Established in that samādhi, one beholds [it] through the power of the supreme Śakti;
the yogi who delights in eternal yoga has no doubt regarding that time.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Timirodghāṭana*.
Chapter Nine: Śakti, the Guru, and the Goddess spoke.

Bhairava said: "How is it that the supreme power (*parāśakti*), once arisen, pervades the three worlds? And how is it that all yogins meditate upon her, who bestows the path to liberation? *Timirodghāṭaṭīkā 9.1ab*: *katham utpannā parāśaktis trailokyavyāpinī katham* *Timirodghāṭaṭīkā 9.1cd*: *dhyāyanti yoginaḥ sarve mokṣamārgapradāyakām* *Bhairava uvāca* (Bhairava said)

O Goddess, you consist of all the gods and stand above all the worlds; you are all-pervading, beginningless, and worshipped among all the deities. Pervading the fourteen worlds, you are situated above the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
TimUdgh 9.3cd: [The deities] consisting of Śiva and Śakti are worshipped in all their forms.
TimUdgh 9.4ab: Seated upon lotus-thrones, they hold rosaries and water-pots.
TimUdgh 9.4cd: Wearing matted hair and bark garments, such is the worship of Brahmā.
TimUdgh 9.5ab: ... they practice yoga.
TimUdgh 9.5cd: Bearing the conch, discus, and mace—thus indeed is Viṣṇu worshipped. TimUdgh 9.6ab:
Therefore, she who holds a skull-topped staff smeared with ashes, radiant with ornaments of skulls...
TimUdgh 9.6cd: O Sulocanā, I indeed assume the form of a naked ascetic.
TimUdgh 9.7ab: O Suśrotrā, what indeed does one see when the mind is constantly fixed upon that?
TimUdgh 9.7cd: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara meditate upon the Supreme Power (Parāśakti).

TimUdgh 9.8ab: All other sages as well, together with the gods, asuras, and yogins, TimUdgh 9.8cd: meditate upon the supreme digit [of the moon], such as Devendra, Candra, Sūrya, and so forth. TimUdgh 9.9ab: O Goddess, why indeed was [this] asked of you in the past by the mighty Dānavas?
TimUdgh 9.9cd: Together with all the Dānavas, they have come to me for refuge. TimUdgh 9.10ab: By me, as well as by all the gods, the Śakti was meditated upon.
TimUdgh 9.10cd: She arrived at that very moment, her mind fixed on the Supreme Power (Parāśakti).
TimUdgh 9.11ab: ...joined with the anus, behold [them] having approached.
TimUdgh 9.11cd: By her, this entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is pervaded.
TimUdgh 9.12ab: Of him... remained... [fol. 36r]
There are hundreds of thousands of Yoginīs, numbering in the millions and tens of millions in manifold ways.
Though she is one, she exists in many forms; having pervaded all, she has reached the supreme state.
She is both the transcendent (*apara*) and the immanent (*aparā*), consisting of the power of touch (*sparśa-śakti*).
The one [Śakti], divided into three parts, is established in many varieties. TimUdgh 9.14ab: ekā tribhedabhinnā sā bahubhedeṣu saṃsthitā.

TimUdgh 9.14cd: For by your grace, one [power] is indeed supreme; as soon as she is born, she possesses great strength. TimUdgh 9.15ab: The second is the intermediate power, which resides in the mouths of the yogins.
The knowledge of meditation and absorption, the instruction on yogic sound (*yoganāda*),
that which effects the entry into the power of Rudra (*rudraśakti*) and the transmission of gnosis—
this is known as the characteristic of the central power (*madhyamāśakti*).
TimUdgh 9.17ab: Through the instruction of the guru, one attains perfection; through practice, the state that grants liberation. TimUdgh 9.17cd:
Within the thirty-two wheels of the Mothers (*mātṛcakra*), the third power (*śakti*)...
TimUdgh 9.18ab: ...may [the Lord] always perform [this] by means of the mantra at some time.
Indeed, these qualities do not bestow the vision of the gods or liberation.
Śakti is the third, and peace has been described to you... [fol.
36v] ...by means of the descent onto the true path, she has entered the lineage of the Yoginīs.
TimUdgh 9.20ab: But because of that [teacher], the jewel of the instruction on bliss is remembered as the *kaula* [tradition].
TimUdgh 9.20cd: Having abandoned the web of philosophical systems (*tattvajāla*), one should seek the *kaulika* meaning through the *tantra*.
That is the root meaning of the Kaula tradition:
"For the sake of accomplishment, [one should seek] a guru who possesses immediate realization;
O Goddess, a guru is difficult to find, and one who is even greater than a guru is exceedingly rare."
The attainment of that very one who has attained liberation is difficult to find;
for such a person is indeed rare even in the Kaula seat (kaulapīṭha), despite great effort.
TimUdgh 9.23ab: Someone who has traveled to many places may wander through the fields and seats (*kṣetrapīṭha*). TimUdgh 9.23cd: Even after twelve years, he does not see [the truth] at all.
TimUdgh 9.24ab: O Goddess, even one who is well-refined and learned in the meaning of many scriptures, [does not see it].
He may wander from sacred seat to sacred seat, but returning with his purpose unfulfilled,
he remains unrefined and foolish, devoid of the meaning of all the scriptures.
Through the Kaula seed-syllable that has been obtained, the accomplishment of the three worlds shines forth.
Thus is the supreme Kaula yoga, the most excellent among all tantras. O Goddess, this *kaula* bestows liberation; it must be guarded again and again.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Timirodghāṭana*,
titled "The Examination of Disciples" (beginning first with the undesired disciple).
Then Bhairava said:
"O Goddess, one should conceal this secret scripture even from one who is very dear."
Nor should she be given to one who is not distinct [from her], nor to those who revile, nor to those who desire what is undesirable.
Like a forest thicket infested by calamity, he is wrathful, has deformed nails, and is deceitful;
he is fickle, harsh, deficient in limbs, treacherous, and consumptive.

One who is diseased, a logician, one who constantly performs rituals, one who observes the vows of others, one with a crow-like voice, one of little learning, one who is envious, and a defiler of the *samaya*—
one born at the end, one who is reckless, greedy, one with dark teeth, and one whose senses are unconquered.

TimUdgh 10.4cd: One who reviles the guru, the gods, the twice-born, and so forth; one who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī*; TimUdgh 10.5ab: A stage-player, a slanderer, and one intent on [the killing of] a *kṣatriya*, a *tāpasa*, or a *gha* (a low-caste person).
TimUdgh 10.5cd: A follower of Tārkṣya, a partisan of Kaṇāda, an atheist, a wolf, a devourer, one who is cruel, and one who has abandoned his own duty;
TimUdgh 10.6ab: One who obstructs others, a servant, a prostitute, and an adulterer;
TimUdgh 10.6cd: ... [even if] pure and consecrated.
TimUdgh 10.7ab: [One should not avoid] disciples who are embraced by another son (or: by another [teacher]).
TimUdgh 10.7cd: [One should accept those who possess] faith, generosity, and have conquered anger... [fol.37v]
TimUdgh 10.8ab: Pure, wise, grateful, with senses calmed; TimUdgh 10.8cd: peaceful in soul, and capable of auspicious power.
Truthful in speech and firm in his vows, patient and energetic; equal toward all beings, he is a man of knowledge free from envy.
TimUdgh 10.10ab: One who is always devoted to the Guru and the Deity, and is skilled in the meaning of all scriptures;
TimUdgh 10.10cd: ... [who is] intent upon the teaching of Śiva;
TimUdgh 10.11ab: A creator of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) [yet] likewise compassionate.

TimUdgh 10.11cd: Attached to those who have attained intoxication [of wisdom], free from craving, and having abandoned greed; TimUdgh 10.12ab: Observing all fasts and restraints, with a disciplined self, he is dear to [the gods].
One who is properly endowed with the vows from the beginning, a virtuous guardian of the commitments (*samaya*),
a hero who pacifies the planetary spirits, pure in soul, a worshiper of the guru,
well-behaved, peaceful, not talkative, a Brahmin, and not of another caste.

One who belongs to the lowest caste (nāntyavarṇaka) is not [eligible] for the time of thirst regarding that which is to be or has become; one should not bestow it upon those among the five [classes] who have not been well-tested.
However, it is beneficial when given to disciples who have been thoroughly examined, in a secret and very firm [place].

TimUdgh 10.15ab: One should cause [these] to be given among these castes; TimUdgh 10.15cd: One should regard wealth, as well as wife, children, and so forth, for the sake of the guru, as if they were mere grass.

Thus, the disciple who conducts himself in this manner and offers everything as his very self—this is the supreme reality of these [teachings]. It should not be disclosed to those who have not received initiation. I have declared this for your sake; it must not be given to one who has not been tested.
TimUdgh 10.17cd: The self is manifold and corrupt; [it is not the] reality of the supreme principle...

TimUdgh 10.18ab: Whether by means of material substance, through illusion, or again by means of ritual service according to dharma, TimUdgh 10.18cd: they perform an offering to the principle, yet they do not delight in the principle itself.
TimUdgh 10.19ab: ... [those] who produce conviction regarding the Self.
TimUdgh 10.19cd: But he whose self is disciplined meditates for twelve days without weariness;
TimUdgh 10.20ab: endowed with [powers] such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, he becomes omniscient.

In the case of a *tṛvakra* [offense], it is for five Brahmins; for a *kṣetriya*, it is for six, seven, or eight. For those who discharge excrement or urine [inappropriately], it is to be given for ten or twelve years. It should be granted even to one who has not been examined, provided he is not a nihilist or a reviler.
One should not act with deceit, nor should it be given to just anyone; rather,
if the Guru is indeed pleased with a disciple who is not unreasonably obstinate,
he should not wait for the prescribed time but should reveal [the secret] immediately.
The Brahmin may be deceitful, but the Mleccha is not deceitful. Even a Mleccha should be given [instruction], but one must not cause [an unfit person] to give it.
The teacher, who is equal to Śiva, should bestow grace upon the world.
When greed for wealth has fully taken hold, yet not so with kinsmen and one's own people,
he will follow the path of the teacher’s [tradition], and through that thread,
he will proceed to the cycle of existence.

Teaching and providing exposition, awakening the teacher and the disciple, as well as [the act of] honoring, should be understood in that way; and having looked upon the teacher for a very long time, one should likewise honor him—this is how it should be known. One should offer [everything] to the teacher and likewise worship the teacher.
TimUdgh 10.27cd: O Goddess, O Beloved, that which does not transfer to another is clearly not to be given. TimUdgh 10.28ab:
O Goddess of good vows, one should not give even a small amount of wealth to a disciple who is unworthy.
Otherwise,
this secret text will perish.
Therefore, this essential text that bestows liberation must not be given away nor should its meaning be disclosed.
Thus ends the tenth chapter on the Dispelling of Darkness.
[Regarding] the Yoga of Wood and the Yoga of Nectar,
the Goddess said:

"O Bhairava, tell me that which bestows liberation, is easily accomplished, possesses superior qualities, and is characterized by both the yoga of wood and the yoga of nectar. Thus [the disciple] spoke.
Bhairava said:
O Dear One, I have previously explained Yoga in its sixfold form with six limbs,
according to its many various divisions, for the sake of meditation, mantra, and other rites. O Goddess, I shall now contemplate the Yoga of Nectar, which is superior even to the work of wood.
Go or stay, or likewise [do] waking or even deep sleep;
or rather, waking and deep sleep.
For one who is devoted to delighting in action, constant yoga proceeds;
yet the mind may be joined elsewhere and the gaze cast elsewhere.
Even so, for the yogin, yoga proceeds without interruption.
For the yogin,
there is neither *dhāraṇā* nor *vedha*, nor *āvāhana* and *visarjana*;
even when in any state whatsoever, or even while playing, [he remains so] for the yogin.
By his own will he dwells in the forest, and by his own will in the midst of people;
by his own will he enjoys worldly pleasures, and by his own will he observes vows.
Where there is freedom from longing, there is yoga, which is devoid of all ritual action.
TiUdgh 11.8ab: O Goddess, there is nothing higher than this which brings such supreme delight to the mind;
TiUdgh 11.8cd: [a teaching] devoid of the syllables of Tantric lore, and lacking meditation and dhāraṇā;
TiUdgh 11.9ab: secret, free from conceptual thought, most subtle, immortal, and supreme.

Thus, O Goddess, the Kaulikas obtain the nectar of yoga; those devoted to the samādhi of nectar shall, through practice, attain that which bestows liberation. Practice leads to the supreme yoga, and the touch of samādhi shall arise.
TiUdgh 11.11ab: The pure one sees again...
[and] TiUdgh 11.11cd: [It is] shaped like a *kadamba* bud, with a radiance equal to ten million suns.
TiUdgh 11.12ab: The yogin, through purity, beholds it situated within the center of the body.
[The yogin] sees [the deity] with the color of a white lotus, or with the splendor of a spear, by means of divine yoga. He sees the yogin situated within the center of the body;
he sees [him] abiding in all bodies, having gone to the state of Brahman.
The Self has gone to the end of the worlds; because it is all-pervading, it extends higher and higher.
O you of good vows, this expansion of the single Kaulika [teaching], which belongs to divine yoga,
is not seen elsewhere among all other yogas or samādhis.
How can that which is being told be unbelievable? What wonder and amazement is there [in this]?
For he who here possesses the divine self-realization on all sides—knowledge that delights in the delusion of existence—is directly perceived within himself.
When direct perception is seen, erroneous cognition perishes.
Thus one perceives the power of Rudra, O beloved of the Guru, within direct perception. O Beloved, that which has been taught regarding the divine yogas is accomplished, O Lord.
TiUdgh 11.18cd: Having obtained a guru who is devoid of power, O Dear One, how can there be the accomplishment of the disciple?
TiUdgh 11.19ab: When the root is destroyed, O Goddess, how can there be flowers, fruits, and so forth from the tree?
TiUdgh 11.19cd: A guru who is permeated by the power of Rudra is the most supreme among gurus.
TiUdgh 11.20ab: He who knows the Self and is joined with the Beloved—that teacher bestows the state of liberation.

TiUdgh 11.20cd: Or rather, all those who have come from the other world bestow liberation once again. TiUdgh 11.21ab: The Kaula tradition provides direct experiential realization both in this world and in the next.
But he who has confidence regarding this life will also accomplish the next world. If there is no confidence regarding this life, how could there be a next world?
When such [a state] is directly perceived...
O Guru, [one should know] the Self as knowledge through the threefold inner self;
[the Guru, however,
is] like the sky for the flight of the two [wings of] faith.

If one desires success for oneself, the Guru is to be worshipped as the supreme object of veneration. The teacher who bestows the divine instruction is as rare as a deity. Where there are many gurus, there is only empty talk and a lack of conviction.
TiUdgh 11.25cd: Some yogins [are] devoid of means of valid knowledge and destroyers of the vital points of others.
TiUdgh 11.26ab: Some, devoid of knowledge, are arrogant due to the neglect of their own physical discipline (*tandava*).
TiUdgh 11.26cd: Some are satisfied with mere mantras, [neglecting] their own small...

TiUdgh 11.27ab: In the case of those born of low or high [castes] and so forth, there is no head [initiation] in the Praṇava of the Teacher. TiUdgh 11.27cd: O Goddess, some teachers declare that he is the one who brings about the destruction of saṃsāra.
TiUdgh 11.28ab: ...how could there be liberation from the wandering [in saṃsāra]?
TiUdgh 11.28cd: Those possessed of passion, hatred, and egoism hate one another.
TiUdgh 11.29ab: O fair-faced one, how could they possess the true essence of Kaulika knowledge?
TiUdgh 11.29cd: [They are] ... incapable.
Others are engaged [in other ways]. It is not appropriate for [these practices] among lineages or castes; they are said to be bestowers of liberation.
O Goddess, without the Kaulika, the divine eye does not arise...
...for them, there shall be the great status of a Kaula master;
and if [the disciple] is incapable of the practice of yoga, the Yoginī should seek [another].
As long as these two [conditions] exist, liberation is not found.
TiUdgh 11.32cd: ... [he is] joined in yoga, however, to that which is Kaulika;
TiUdgh 11.33ab: "Thus, yoga is born as superior, possessing the excellence of all sovereign qualities.
Thus ends the eleventh [chapter] in the *Timirodghāṭana*.
The Goddess said:
"In this introduction to yoga, however, the yogas have been presented in their sequential order;
[now tell me] about the worship of the *liṅga* for them, as well as the mantras, tantras, syllables, and so forth."
Having thoroughly purified the Guru, he should explain everything to the disciple: Parā,
Sūkṣmā, and then Paramā, according to how they may be experienced.

TiUdgh 12.3ab: But its gross state is said to be... [omitted] ... TiUdgh 12.3cd: O sons, the supreme state of liberation is to be known as divine and auspicious. TiUdgh 12.4ab: For them, there is no linga made of clay, nor one of stone, silver, or gold.
TiUdgh 12.4cd: Not the variegated [liṅga], nor one’s own body...
TiUdgh 12.5ab: The liṅga within one’s own bodies is to be worshipped; it is the great abode of merit and dharma. TiUdgh 12.5cd: He who... has been described [attains] both enjoyment and liberation.
...and for the yogin,
his worship is performed by one below;
...it brings about liberation and the accomplishment of one's desires.
The Lord of Yoga, according to his desire...
even for him there is liberation...
there is no going elsewhere for him; such is the conviction of the world.

Thus, the Supreme Power, presiding over the entire universe situated within the womb of the cosmic egg, makes it all [manifest]; yet she herself remains partless. She is the Linga, presiding over every yogin.
The self-realized direct perception rests upon both the differentiated and the undifferentiated;
it rests upon all the deities;
it encompasses all thirty [principles] and is the direct cognition of everything.
TiUdgh 12.12cd: The divine one who sees the god in the sky and in the intermediate space...
TiUdgh 12.13ab: ...as well as in clay or wood, in a *liṅga* or even in an image;
TiUdgh 12.13cd: by those human yogins, through that which has the form of the characteristics of a person (*pudgala*).
The yogin established in the divine eye perceives...
[41v] For him whose divine state is attained, what need is there for images? They perceive the supreme knowledge of the three worlds through the divine signs.

TiUdgh 12.15cd: What does it do? It is the *liṅga* [of that] whose...ness [it is]. TiUdgh 12.16ab: Residing within the body, it knows the cosmic egg (*brāhmāṇḍa*) as arising from the interior of the three worlds.
TiUdgh 12.16cd: O Lord of Yogins, one should always worship this great-souled *liṅga*.
And the reflection is [in] you...
but it is not direct perception; O Goddess, without the nectar, the lord of yogins does not attain the supreme state through the successive application of wood.
Like a woman devoid of shame,
she delights as she pleases in a lonely, lovely, or secret place;
like a woman longing for her limbs, she [clings] to the body.
Rama... & ... for one who is passionately attached, she is a beloved who brings the bliss of passion;
yet she also leads to dispassion.
...and the *dhikaulakī* indeed...
[it is] that which produces immediate realization...
all [of this].
"Truth, truth, again...
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Darkness," from the *Jñānasūla*.

Viṣṇu is proclaimed as established in the power of action (kriyā-śakti); Umāsoma is proclaimed as established in the power of will (icchā-śakti); [and] Śaktiśiva... [is established in the power of knowledge].
The nāḍī on the left is proclaimed as the Śakti Brāhmī; Suṣumnā, situated in the middle, is to be known as the Śakti Jyeṣṭhā; and Piṅgalā is likewise proclaimed.

This is declared to be the "Spear of Knowledge" (jñānaśūla), endowed with the three powers; having pierced the moon, the sun, and the third mandala of fire, it is established as the three lines... [ta].
Whether upon ashes or in water, one should deposit [the deity] with the spear of knowledge;
he who worships the Lord of the Self-born (Svāyambhuva) in the midst of the fire [conquers] the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
Those who have gone there obtain that fruit;
he who should sacrifice at Somatīrtha performs the protection of the body of the Self-Existent (Svayambhū), and by him all is honored. Niṣkala...
If one were to give the entire Pātāla, half the earth, and the moon at midday,
filled with jewels, to a yogi of praised vows,
they would obtain that same fruit by offering a single flower upon their own body.
When he had established [the teaching] in purity, the people [worshipped] the Lord of the Three Worlds; through the absence of passion, [he attained] the state of detachment,
reaching the ultimate limit.
And having offered praise, one who gives a full measure of jewels to the preceptor—
ten million times ten million times— [is equal to one] in the body and in the flower of Śiva.
Twofold when combined with fragrance, and fourfold by means of incense; through the attainment of fragrant flowers, another [attains] the heart. Māṃ.
...by the desire for the mantra-words of the Ṣṭhi...piva [deity],
he [attains] that which is perfectly stainless.
The knower of yoga should join himself there with the thread... he should drink the *laṃ*...
the mantra.
One does not fear even among those who take life;
[one is freed from] thousands of killings of Brahmins and hundreds of horse-sacrifices... [even] by other sins committed.
Having yoked the self, they say that Brahmā is like a balance.
Oṃ, homage to Śiva.
The Goddess said:
That which is thus partless... [and] that which is partless, stainless, peaceful, free from conceptual proliferation, and without characteristics.
Inconceivable, unknowable, devoid of destruction and origination,
absolute, solitary, peaceful, pure...
the instrument liberated from yoga, free from causes and means of proof.
At that very moment they are liberated. O Śaṅkara, tell me that knowledge wherein power is space, which resides within the body yet is devoid of the body—
how [is it] in the body?
How is it devoid of a body?
How does the *jīva* abide within the body? O *jīva*, why is it proclaimed as "living"?
By what does this *jīva* live, and by what path does it move?
How can the soul, which is all-pervading, become a "necklace" (niṣka)?
How does this soul see? What is the food of the soul?
Where does the soul dissolve? And who indeed is born here?
Of what color and of what measure is the soul?
Tell me all this, O God of gods, Maheśvara,
Lord of Light, who grants liberation from the beginning from the bonds of the ocean of worldly existence.
The Lord said:

Then wind and fire are designated as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the individual soul should be understood as white, conceived as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, as long as it is joined with existence.
When joined with that [planet] presided over by Rāja (Mars), Jīva (Jupiter) will certainly become black;
when Jīva is joined with Sattva (Mercury), [the results] are as follows.
But when joined with passion,
and likewise joined with delusion, one then proceeds toward evil;
[the nose-tip is not...]
[The syllable] *tu* [is placed] in the heart-lotus; moreover, it is held both below and above.
...the dharma...
and the vital breath (prāṇa) are to be known as established as far as the tip of the nose;
situated there, it is declared to be partless (niṣkala), for as long as one continues to breathe.
Joined with a thousand breaths, it then dissolves into the space within the heart; having thus attained partlessness,
the third breath of the living being is proclaimed.
By means of the beautiful ray [of light] from the heart-lotus, [the breath] moves downward...
"That very life-force is brought under control," so it was said by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
O Goddess, as long as there is no exhalation, so long is it called "partless" (niṣkala).
O Goddess, there is no exhaling;
knowing [the Self] as non-abiding and partless, [one should know] the path...
situated in the navel for all activities, and situated in the heart, free from activity.
Situated within the mouth and nostrils, the Lord experiences the sense objects;
the individual soul (jīva), residing in the body, sees, smells, hears,
and experiences both the auspicious and the inauspicious, established as it is in body after body.
When the living being, having abandoned the body, has resorted to the external space,
then the living being becomes devoid of an object.
That very [state] is the fearless Brahman; having meditated upon that, he becomes Sadāśiva.
Having meditated upon Śiva, the unborn and eternal, one is released from the cage of sins. Ananta, who resides within all bodies, perceives Śiva situated at the tip of the nose.
...of all beings, they are seen; yet it does not move for one who has attained stability.
The Goddess, situated in the center of the navel, is utterly stainless as the reality of accomplishment (*siddhitattva*).
She blazes intensely like the sun, and her bones are set ablaze.
...and the eighth seed-syllable called *jīva*, which resides within the body;
by means of this, [the body] is pervaded and rendered impure, like milk...
grasped by the instruments consisting of the self, along with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the life-force (*prāṇa*), and their respective limbs—the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—...
Through the union of inhalation and exhalation, it dissolves downward and upward,

just as a dry leaf is carried by the wind; in this manner, that which is called the "living soul" (jīva), known as the vital breath (prāṇa) and its opposite (aprāṇa), wanders within the tree of worldly existence.

The individual soul (*jīva*), joined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and its counterpart (*aprāṇa*), likewise resides in the heart. [It is joined with] inhalation and exhalation... [and] endowed with merit and demerit.

The Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is perceived through the power of *śakti*—[the sequence of phonemes: *śa*, *kta*, *nā*, *da*, *re*, *cā*, *ne*, *ca*, *dṛ*, *śya*. *(Note: The bottom lines of the manuscript are missing; the provided text ends at this point.)*
...it has emerged;
it is renowned as Siddhakaula, and it is devoid of downward movement.
And indeed one's own [relatives],
and especially those who have fallen away.

Those who have resorted to the yoga of Akula attain the state beyond old age and death, which is all-pervading; they obtain the wheel that has arrived, the mandala-sovereignty, and the bowing [of all beings].
And likewise, the wise one should always worship even a single sandalwood footstool as his own self;
for by that which is proclaimed as the Ocean of Kula, there is the granting of liberation from the cycle of saṃsāra.
O Lord, you who bring an end to the Kali Yuga at the conclusion of the four ages,
this divine Kaula [tradition] of yours shall never perish;
by it all is eternally pervaded...

But the root is indeed one, while its branches are manifold; by the power of that root, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings grows forth. Established in the single reality, it remains uniform in its essential nature.

Pervasive as the sky, infinite, stainless, and the Lord, He is the cause; at the end of the stainless, He is the eternal, immovable form. He is called "selfless" because His nature is like various spaces and devoid of conventional conduct.

Free from the six letters, supported by the supportless reality, having the form of a movement within intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and being the essence-mass within intrinsic nature— the yogi who is eternally capable should always accomplish the supreme mass (*piṇḍa*).
United with the single hermitage and dwelling in a single place,
she does not go to the sacred seats (pīṭhas) nor to the fields of offering (balikṣetra);
for the seats and fields reside within the body, and she does not wander to other fields.
Wherever the sequence of Bali and Vahni occurs, there arises that which originates from the Kula;
it is the support of the Kula, the Kula, the seat (pīṭha), and Akula, the protector of the field (kṣetrapālaka).
It is neither the assembly of Yoginīs nor the sequential procedure of the conduct (caryāvidhi).
The great union of Śiva and Śakti is called the divine union;
it is not the wearing of the meditation-band, nor the carrying of the yoga-staff,
nor indeed the shaving of the hair, nor the wearing of the girdle of muñja grass and so forth.
There is no need for a loincloth or a vow, nor for the concealment of outward signs;
there is no ritual at the junctions of time (saṃdhyā), no fire-ritual, and no materials for oblations and the like.
For the great sacrificial pit resides within the body, a blazing mandala of fire.
Resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, possessing a radiance equal to the brilliance of lightning,
[the Lord of Yogins who is joined with a hundred commitments] has a mind that is the very essence of the world;
he has attained that which is reached through the non-sequential path and is not differentiated by clan.
...the avoidance of the established doctrine of Bhairava-vrata with effort, [which is] abiding in a state of single form.
Just as all those [waters] enter into the ocean... so it is with them.
When the Great Path is seen, there is no doubt regarding all reality;
reality abides in a single form, established as both the pervaded and the pervader. This is the divine Kaula, endowed with Śiva and Śakti.

One should worship the Siddhas and Yoginīs who reside in all the sacred seats (pīṭhas) according to the Kula path; for this divine Kula, which is the supreme seat, pervades and has been attained through that which abides in the void.
For him, there are no mechanical devices or mantras; he perceives the equality within the accomplishment of the constellations and mantras.
The entire world of speech, including the moving and the unmoving, is seen as equal.
Being free from passion through equanimity, he remains indifferent with a peaceful mind.
Likewise, that which has issued from the mouth [of the teacher], being concentrated through devotion to the guru, one should always maintain its observance; established in the state of a single form,
then that very Kaula nature arrives, and one shall attain the state of Nirvāṇa.
The yogi shall attain that state of nirvāṇa through unceasing practice; established in the state beyond conduct,
he attains liberation among all principles— liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra.

When the state of agelessness and immortality is pervaded, then there is liberation, without a doubt; the yogin becomes a divine body, free from wrinkles and grey hair. He wanders through the expanse of the sky, together with gods, asuras, and humans.
Furthermore, they are not bound, like a lotus leaf by water;
this pure and divine [teaching], which removes the darkness of the bound souls,
is the Siddhakaula that must be known, as spoken by Siddhanātha.
It does not abide in the center between the moon and the sun, nor likewise in fire or wind;
it is to be reached through instruction, established within the mouth of the Guru,
free from conceptual construction, and has emerged from the illustrious face.
Infinite, stainless, and peaceful, devoid of causes and characteristics—
this Yoga, so difficult to attain, was taught by the Lord of Fishes (Mīnanātha).
This *Yogasadbhāva* is completed.
Bhairava said:
It is not in the navel nor in the heart, nor indeed in the throat nor in the palate;
O lady of excellent hips, it is not found in the forehead nor at the tip of the uvula.
There is no liberation through the flow into the *brahmarandhra*, nor is there any means [to attain it];
there is no duality of the mind at the *dvādaśānta*, nor is there any cultivation by the mind through the principle of reality; there is no liberation, nor does it exist.
O Varārohā, there may be some conceptualization regarding the kinsman of the intellect, yet within the secret [place],
no [such thing] exists at all.
O fair-faced one, the garland of impurities as well as the color and the life-force (jīvaśakti) must be uttered in the form of all the principles (tattvas); for them, there is no liberation.

O illustrious Great Goddess, having known that knot which is both supreme and non-supreme in the form of gnosis, one seizes the eye, ear, nose, mouth, and hands— the other [sensory] knowledge— and thus attains the excellent state.
O Goddess, Mistress of the Gods, having known the divine channel by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded,
one should practice inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), but one should avoid the third, exhalation (*recaka*), O Goddess, if one desires supreme accomplishment.
One should avoid those things, O Goddess, if one desires accomplishment...
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristic of reality (*tattva*):
it is neither conscious nor insentient, and likewise, it is neither the self (*ātman*) nor another.
Śrīdhāriṇī, who is the all-knowing one perfected in the state of fullness,
is neither empty nor perceptible, neither distant nor in the middle;
Śrīdhāriṇī, who is the all-knowing one perfected in the state of fullness.
Neither in the body nor in space, nor even in that which has become dissolved, nor indeed anywhere else— this state which is utterly liberated is the Kaulika state; it is considered the Kaulika.
Having abandoned these states, those who know the state of fullness—the state filled with great bliss—are the true practitioners of the Kaula tradition.
They have entered into a single form, peaceful, [realizing] the reality that is both supreme and non-supreme. ||| Orn |||

Just as the goddess Vipulā was awakened at that very moment, O Goddess,
so too is the living soul (jīva) when it is enveloped by merit and demerit through the yoga of knowledge and discernment, O Goddess.
...the venerable Śiva and the Goddess are written but not recited;
when [the breath] has emerged from the two cavities, O son of Vāyu, it dissolves. That is liberation, the Supreme Brahman, that Śiva, the supreme state.

That which is supremely subtle at the tip of the mouth, seen in the midst of space— O lady of excellent countenance, having established the mind there, meditate upon that supreme middle [state] where the breath, having emerged from the nostrils, is dissolved.

That Śiva is indeed *ṛtti*, and he is the bestower of liberation from liberation; he is declared to be established at the tip of the nose when one breathes while reciting the mantra. — *Nirvāṇakārikā*
